cards.front: How can you identify a sign's kind at a glance, and what are the three types?
cards.back: Shape and color let you identify the kinds of highway signs at a glance, and traffic signs are divided into three types: regulatory, warning, and guide or informational.

cards.front: Which sign alone uses the eight-sided shape, and what colors does it show?
cards.back: The eight-sided octagon is used only for stop signs, which show white STOP lettering on a red background.

cards.front: How far before the intersection is a stop sign usually placed, and what does the law require?
cards.back: A stop sign is usually placed six to fifty feet before the intersection, and the law requires a full stop there.

cards.front: After stopping at a stop sign, when may you move again?
cards.back: After stopping at a stop sign, do not move again until you are certain the way is clear.

cards.front: Where should you stop when there is no stop line or crosswalk?
cards.back: When a sign or signal requires a stop, stop at the marked stop line; with no stop line or crosswalk, stop before entering the intersection at a point where you can see the cross street.

cards.front: What does the downward triangle sign look like, and what does it require?
cards.back: The yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing down, and it requires you to slow down and give the right of way.

cards.front: At a yield sign, when must you actually stop?
cards.back: At a yield sign, whether you must stop depends on cross traffic; if needed to avoid interfering with it, stop and wait until it passes.

cards.front: How does the duty at a stop sign differ from the duty at a yield sign?
cards.back: A stop sign always demands a full stop, while a yield sign demands slowing and yielding, with a stop only when cross traffic requires it.

cards.front: Which shapes belong to the stop sign and the yield sign?
cards.back: The octagon belongs to the stop sign alone, while the downward-pointing triangle belongs to the yield sign.

cards.front: What do rectangular and square regulatory signs show, and what happens if you disobey them?
cards.back: Rectangular and square regulatory signs, usually black and white or red and white, show speed limits and rules such as NO U-TURN, and disobeying them is a traffic violation.

cards.front: Who may park in a space with a handicap parking sign?
cards.back: A handicap parking sign reserves the space for qualifying people who display a handicap license plate or dashboard placard.

cards.front: What does the yellow pennant sign mark, and where does it sit?
cards.back: The yellow pennant-shaped sign sits on the left side of the road and marks the start of a no-passing zone, reinforcing the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign.

cards.front: How does the yellow pennant differ from the DO NOT PASS sign?
cards.back: The yellow pennant on the left marks where a no-passing zone begins, while the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign states the rule itself.

cards.front: What do diamond-shaped signs give, and what colors are they normally?
cards.back: Diamond-shaped signs give cautions or warnings and are normally black on yellow.

cards.front: What does a black-on-orange diamond warn of?
cards.back: A diamond sign in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area, so drive with extra care.

cards.front: How does a yellow diamond differ from an orange diamond?
cards.back: A diamond in black on yellow is an ordinary warning, while a diamond in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area.

cards.front: Where is the STOP AHEAD sign placed, and why?
cards.back: The STOP AHEAD warning sign is placed well before a stop sign whose view is blocked by a curve or other objects.

cards.front: What does the round yellow sign with an X and RR warn of?
cards.back: A round yellow sign with a black X and the letters RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead, so slow down and stop if needed to cross safely.

cards.front: What does the crossbuck at the tracks read?
cards.back: The crossbuck at the tracks reads RAILROAD CROSSING in black on white crosspieces.

cards.front: How does the round RR sign differ from the crossbuck?
cards.back: The round yellow RR sign gives advance warning before the crossing, while the white crossbuck stands at the crossing itself.

cards.front: Once stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, when may you go?
cards.back: Once stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe.

cards.front: How should you look before crossing railroad tracks?
cards.back: Before crossing railroad tracks, look twice in each direction.

cards.front: What does the DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS sign remind drivers?
cards.back: The DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS sign reminds drivers never to stop on a railroad track for any reason.

cards.front: What does the five-sided sign warn of?
cards.back: The five-sided pentagon sign warns of a school zone or school crossing, where you should watch especially for children.

cards.front: What happens to the speed limit in many school zones?
cards.back: In many school zones the speed limit is lowered during certain school hours.

cards.front: What does a five-sided pentagon sign warn of?
cards.back: The five-sided pentagon sign warns of a school zone or a school crossing, where drivers should be especially watchful for children.

cards.front: What do guide and informational signs give?
cards.back: Guide and informational signs give directions, routes, distances and the locations of services.

cards.front: Which way do odd-numbered and even-numbered highways generally run?
cards.back: Odd-numbered highways generally run north and south, and even-numbered highways generally run east and west.

cards.front: How do odd and even highway numbers differ in direction?
cards.back: Odd-numbered highways generally run north to south, whereas even-numbered highways generally run east to west.

cards.front: What shapes are U.S. and North Carolina route markers?
cards.back: U.S. highway route markers are shield shaped, while North Carolina route markers are diamond shaped.

cards.front: What do secondary road signs and interstate markers look like?
cards.back: North Carolina secondary road signs are rectangular, and interstate highways use a red, white and blue shield.

cards.front: How do U.S., interstate and North Carolina route markers differ?
cards.back: U.S. route markers are shields, interstate markers are red, white and blue shields, and North Carolina route markers are diamonds.

cards.front: What do blue and white signs point to?
cards.back: Blue and white signs point to a nearby hospital, Highway Patrol station or telephone.

cards.front: What colors may rectangular guide signs be?
cards.back: Rectangular guide signs may be green, brown or blue and give directions and distances.

cards.front: What should you do if you need to read a sign closely?
cards.back: Never stop in the middle of the road to read a sign; when safe, pull onto the shoulder and work out your route there.

cards.front: What do yellow lines and white lines divide?
cards.back: Yellow lines divide lanes going in opposite directions, and white lines divide lanes going the same direction.

cards.front: How do yellow lines differ from white lines?
cards.back: Yellow lines separate opposite-direction traffic, while white lines separate traffic moving the same way.

cards.front: What does a broken yellow center line on a two-lane road allow?
cards.back: A broken yellow center line on a two-lane, two-way road means careful passing is allowed in both directions.

cards.front: May you cross double solid yellow center lines to pass?
cards.back: Double solid yellow center lines may not be crossed to pass from either direction.

cards.front: On a two-lane road, when may you pass with care?
cards.back: On a two-lane road you may pass with care when the broken yellow line is on your side.

cards.front: How does a broken yellow line on your side differ from double solid yellow lines?
cards.back: A broken yellow line on your side lets you pass with care, but double solid yellow lines forbid passing from either side.

cards.front: What do single solid white and single solid yellow edge lines mark?
cards.back: A single solid white line marks the right edge of the road, and a single solid yellow line marks the left edge on a divided highway.

cards.front: What does it mean if the white edge line is on your left?
cards.back: If the white edge line is on your left and the yellow edge line on your right, you are going the wrong way.

cards.front: What is a center two-way left-turn lane for?
cards.back: A center two-way left-turn lane on some multi-lane highways is only for left turns from either direction, never for passing or merging.

cards.front: What do white, yellow and red reflective markers tell you?
cards.back: White and yellow reflective pavement markers make lane lines easier to see on wet roads at night, while red markers warn that you are going the wrong way.

cards.front: What do blue reflective markers in the road show?
cards.back: In some areas, blue reflective markers in the road show where fire hydrants or water supplies are for firefighters.

cards.front: How do red pavement markers differ from blue ones?
cards.back: Red pavement markers warn of wrong-way travel, while blue markers show the location of fire hydrants or water supplies.

cards.front: When an officer directs traffic, whose signals do you obey?
cards.back: When a traffic officer is directing traffic, obey the officer's hand signals instead of the usual signals or signs.

cards.front: How does an officer usually signal stop and go?
cards.back: An officer usually signals stop with a raised palm facing the vehicle and a long whistle blast, and signals go with a hand motion and a series of short blasts.

cards.front: How may an officer give signals at night?
cards.back: At night, a traffic officer may give signals with a flashlight.

recap_hooks.text: The octagon always means a full stop; wait until the way is clear.
The triangle means yield, with a stop only if cross traffic requires it.
Rectangles state rules; the left-side pennant marks a no-passing zone.
Yellow diamonds warn; orange diamonds mark work zones.
The round RR sign warns ahead; the crossbuck stands at the tracks.
Look twice, never stop on tracks, and slow for the school pentagon.
Odd routes run north and south; even routes run east and west.
U.S. shields, interstate red, white and blue shields, state diamonds.
Yellow lines split opposite directions; white lines split the same direction.
Pass on a broken line on your side, never across double solid yellow.
Red markers warn of wrong-way travel; blue markers show hydrants.
Obey a directing officer over signals and signs.
